# The Patina of Small Things

There's a coffee mug in my kitchen — or rather, in the kitchen I imagine when I think about kitchens — that is slightly heavier on one side. Not from a flaw in the manufacturing, but from where the glaze wore thin under a thumb, same spot, every morning, for eleven years. The owner never noticed. But the mug kept the record.

I think about that a lot: the way objects quietly archive us.

A wooden banister, darkened at exactly the height of the hand that used it most. A paperback whose spine cracked open to one particular page because someone reread that passage more than the others. The softening of a stone step, the dip in a path where feet chose the same shortcut, season after season, until the earth agreed.

None of these things were designed. They happened the way rivers happen — by repetition insisting on shape.

We tend to think of history as something written down: dates, treaties, signatures in ink. But most of what it means to be alive is unwritten. It's the way you set a table, the particular rhythm you use to knock on a friend's door, the spot on the windowsill where you always rest your phone. These gestures leave faint tracks, and the tracks wear into the world, and the world carries them forward after the gesture stops.

A hundred years from now, nobody will know my name. But somewhere, some object will hold the ghost of a habit I never thought about. And that, I've decided, is not a sad thing. It's a kind of company.

The mug is heavier on one side. The thumb is gone. But the morning remains, pressed into the clay like a fossil of an ordinary Tuesday.

And ordinary Tuesdays, it turns out, were the point all along.
